question: m12
q: Is electricity inflation running ahead of overall inflation?

transcript.answer:
**Yes. Electricity prices are rising much faster than prices overall, though the gap has shrunk a lot since early 2026.**

**Latest figures (August 2026, change from a year earlier, ABS monthly CPI):**
- Electricity: **+13.2%**
- All prices (headline CPI): **+4.0%**

So electricity inflation is about three times the headline rate.

**How it has moved (change from a year earlier):**

| Period | Electricity | All prices |
|---|---|---|
| Jan–Jun 2025 | −5.9% to −13.2% | 1.9%–2.4% (Apr–Jun) |
| Jul 2025 | +13.6% | 3.0% |
| Oct 2025 | +37.1% | 3.8% |
| Feb 2026 | +37.0% (joint peak) | 3.7% |
| Jun 2026 | +22.4% | 3.8% |
| Jul 2026 | +6.1% | 3.5% |
| Aug 2026 | +13.2% | 4.0% |

**What this means:**
- **It's partly a measurement effect.** In the first half of 2025, electricity prices were falling compared with a year earlier. Government bill rebates are the likely reason: the CPI counts them as lower prices. As the rebates shrank or ended, measured prices jumped. So the 20–37% rises from mid-2025 to mid-2026 overstate how much the underlying power price went up. I haven't checked the rebate timing against official sources.
- **The surge is fading.** The sharp drop to 6.1% in July 2026 fits with the big July 2025 jump falling out of the year-on-year comparison. That's also when annual retail price resets usually take effect. August bounced back up to 13.2%, though, so electricity is still clearly running ahead.
- **It's adding to overall inflation.** Headline inflation has stayed around 3.5–4.6% since late 2025, above the RBA's 2–3% target band. Electricity has been one of the bigger contributors.

Monthly CPI figures for single items like electricity can jump around, so the next few releases will show whether it settles closer to the overall rate.
